editorials.heading: Why it matters
editorials.title: A golden fortnight for Swiss sport
paras: Three athletics titles in Birmingham and a newly-crowned football champion (Thun) reaching a guaranteed European league phase is an unusual concentration of success for a small nation in a single quiet mid-summer week — and the athletics, in particular, reads as more than a one-off given the spread of disciplines and the calibre of the athletes beaten.

English football is realigning as the season opens. Arsenal are champions and looked the part; Manchester City are starting again under Enzo Maresca after a decade of Guardiola and may be about to lose Rodri, the holding midfielder around whom their dominance was built. The Community Shield is only a curtain-raiser, but the direction of travel it hinted at — Arsenal setting the pace, City rebuilding — is the story the Premier League will spend the autumn testing.

editorials.heading: Cross-cutting threads
editorials.title: 1. "AI scientist" ships and gets a reality check in the same week
paras: Three of the week's papers push autonomous research agents hard — and one Nature editorial pushes back just as hard. A DeepMind-style team released Faraday, a 27-billion-parameter agent post-trained specifically to replicate research papers, and reports it beating Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks (arXiv:2608.13331). A separate group put seven frontier models through 36 long-horizon R&D tasks and reached a soberer verdict: today's agents "operate more like engineering optimizers than fully autonomous researchers" — they implement and combine established techniques competently, but genuine methodological novelty "remains rare," and their best runs are unstable from attempt to attempt (arXiv:2608.13417). Nature's own comment desk landed on the same beat with the blunt title AI isn't ready to research itself (Nature, 13 Aug 2026). The honest synthesis for a technical reader: the replication frontier is moving fast — turning a paper into working code is now largely automatable, and that alone is a real productivity change — but replication is not discovery, and every careful evaluation this week says the discovery gap is still wide. Watch for the first agent that produces a genuinely novel, independently-verified method rather than a slick recombination; on this week's evidence it hasn't happened, and the labs shipping "AI scientists" and the journals reviewing them agree on that even as their headlines diverge.

2. Symmetry and algebra, not architecture, decide what a network learns. A striking cluster of theory papers this week all locate a model's behaviour in an underlying mathematical structure rather than in the wiring diagram. Neural Quadratic Forms shows that a single symmetry — a layer is a sum over interchangeable units, so relabelling them changes nothing — forces perceptrons, attention layers, mixtures-of-experts and convolutions into one minimal model, differing only by a "structure matrix," and that this model predicts both the abrupt step-like plateaus of learning and the smooth power-law loss curves as two limits of the same dynamics (arXiv:2608.13335). Algebraic Decomposition Theory proves that whether a transformer generalises to longer sequences than it trained on is governed by an algebraic property of the task — one that classical decomposition theory for finite systems literally cannot see (arXiv:2608.13433). And an interpretability study finds that a model represents "false" and "impossible" as near-orthogonal directions in its activation space — geometry encoding a distinction philosophers have argued over for centuries (arXiv:2608.12852). The through-line: as the field's empirical zoo of architectures keeps growing, the explanatory action is moving the other way — toward the small set of symmetries, algebras and geometries that many architectures secretly share. It is the most encouraging sign in a while that deep learning might acquire a real theory rather than a bestiary.

3. Deep time as data for the present — and it is not an abstraction this week. While Switzerland lives through a scorching, rain-starved August, a Nature paper reconstructs a medieval catastrophe with an uncomfortably direct message: in 1341–1343, sixteen major floods cascaded across Europe, four of them 500-to-1,000-year events, making 1342 the worst flood year of the past seven centuries (Nature, 12 Aug 2026). The lesson the authors draw is precisely the one flood-risk managers resist — that the recent instrumental record badly understates what is physically possible. The same "read the deep past to bound the present" move runs through the week's biology: a Nature Review traces the machinery of human antiviral immunity — cGAS–STING, inflammasomes, viperin — back billions of years to bacterial anti-phage defences (Nature, 12 Aug 2026), and a Quanta feature revisits the old, contested idea that aging is a program rather than mere wear-and-tear (Quanta, 14 Aug 2026). The connective idea worth carrying: for both climate risk and biological mechanism, the historical and evolutionary record is not colour — it is the widest dataset we have, and this week it kept saying the present is narrower than the possible.

4. Quantum's near-term turn: do more with a single qubit. Two results converge on making minimal quantum resources do outsized work. A Harvard–Cornell team proves and experimentally demonstrates that coupling one controllable qubit to an ordinary sensor can exponentially cut the number of measurements needed to learn a classical signal — a 10⁷-fold reduction in the lab for Fourier-amplitude sensing (arXiv:2608.13521). In parallel, Preskill and collaborators show you can prepare the thermal and ground states quantum chemistry needs using a single reusable ancilla qubit as an artificial "bath," with rigorous mixing-time guarantees (Nature Physics, 12 Aug 2026). Both are explicitly framed for "early fault-tolerant" hardware — the messy, few-qubit machines we actually have, not the million-qubit ones we don't. The shape to watch: quantum advantage is quietly being re-scoped from "wait for the big machine" to "wring provable wins out of one good qubit."

stories.headline: An AI system nudges the matrix-multiplication exponent to a new record
stories.summary: The matrix-multiplication exponent ω is the theoretical yardstick for how fast two n×n matrices can in principle be multiplied: schoolbook multiplication costs about n³ operations (ω = 3), and sixty years of algorithm design has been chipping ω down toward the conjectured floor of 2. The current record comes from the "laser method," a technical optimization procedure at the heart of these algorithms. This DeepMind-led team reformulated that optimization so it could be solved in a larger setting, handed it to modern machine-learning solvers, then refined the result with AlphaEvolve (DeepMind's LLM-driven algorithm-discovery system), improving the bound from ω < 2.371339 to ω < 2.371177.
stories.why: the improvement is tiny — it lands in the fifth decimal place and buys no faster software today, since these "galactic" algorithms are far too intricate to run in practice. What's notable is who moved it: an AI system advancing one of theoretical computer science's most-studied constants, on a frontier where human experts have made gains this small over many years.

stories.headline: Iran voids US talks deadline as Hormuz stays shut
stories.summary: Iran declared the 60-day negotiating deadline from its June memorandum with Washington "null and void" on Tuesday 18 August, as a merchant vessel was struck in the Strait of Hormuz and Donald Trump publicly threatened to bomb Oman, the country trying to mediate. Iranian foreign-ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the timeline for a lasting settlement under the June Iran–US memorandum of understanding (a written framework the two sides signed to pause fighting and negotiate) had been rendered void by "violations" he attributed to the United States. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO — the British navy's shipping-incident desk) reported that a vessel transiting the strait early Tuesday was hit by an "unknown projectile" that damaged its engine room and caused one crew casualty, with the Omani coastguard assisting; who fired it is still unestablished. Crossings through Hormuz — the chokepoint carrying roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil — are now in the single digits per day, down from more than 130 before the US and Israel began their war on Iran, and Trump, who has called on Iran to "surrender," used an expletive in threatening to strike Oman if it "gets in the way."
stories.why: a formally abandoned negotiating track plus a fresh strike on shipping points away from de-escalation, and a near-shut Hormuz keeps upward pressure on global oil and freight costs that feed directly into European energy and import prices.

stories.headline: Weak prompt cues can be stacked to strongly control a model
stories.summary: The authors describe a phenomenon they call model hypnosis: individually weak, seemingly irrelevant choices in a prompt — paraphrases, typos, innocuous wording — can be combined so that together they systematically steer a model's behaviour. They report it across model families and scales, including in frontier reasoning models, and find that a "hypnotic" prompt tuned on one model often transfers to another.
stories.why: if inconspicuous surface features can be composed into strong control, that cuts against both safety and interpretability — the levers that move a model are precisely the ones a human reviewer would dismiss as noise, and they generalise across systems rather than staying model-specific. It reframes prompt-based jailbreaks as an additive, transferable effect rather than a bag of one-off tricks.

stories.headline: A memory that starts small keeps long-context models from clogging
stories.summary: Standard attention costs grow quadratically with context length, so a growing line of work compresses the past into a fixed-size "memory state" instead. The snag: with a static memory the earliest tokens face no compression pressure, so they hog degrees of freedom and "pollute" the state, leaving little room for later context. Proteus introduces incremental memory activation — the memory's usable capacity is expanded gradually as the sequence grows. An early bottleneck forces the model to compress history harder; unlocking fresh capacity later reduces interference with new tokens. It drops into several recent memory architectures (Titans, Comba, Hope-Attention) at no added cost, with gains that widen at longer context lengths.
stories.why: long-context recall is where sub-quadratic ("linear-attention") models usually break down; scheduling when memory becomes available, rather than how much there is, is a cheap and broadly reusable lever for that failure mode.

stories.headline: Statistical mechanics predicts how crowds of AI agents drift
stories.summary: As AI agents increasingly talk to each other rather than work alone, their interactions can sharpen collective reasoning — or produce herding and shared bias. The authors ran over 10,000 communities of language-model agents that repeatedly exchange messages and revise their views, on objective maths questions and on subjective political statements. Despite huge variety, the dynamics collapse into three regimes — indifference, polarization, consensus — with agents starting indifferent and building conviction as they interact. On factual questions, talking improves group accuracy; on subjective ones, it tends to drift the group's stated opinion rightward. They fit a statistical-mechanics model (borrowed from physics: agents stochastically favour lower "social pressure," like particles settling toward low energy) that predicts individual trajectories from initial opinions alone and generalises to unseen community structures.
stories.why: it offers compact, testable laws for multi-agent behaviour instead of case-by-case anecdotes — useful for designing agent systems that resist groupthink. The rightward political-drift finding is the authors' own measured result on their setup, and worth treating as a specific empirical claim rather than a general law.

stories.headline: Coding agents fail when the needed fact is not in front of them
stories.summary: Repository-scale coding asks an agent to keep tests, imports, configuration and migration rules mutually consistent inside a limited context window. The authors model each edit as needing a "fact" that comes either from recent context or from the model's baked-in ("parametric") memory; facts supplied by neither channel are coherence debt. Testing seven models across five agent harnesses, they find: no model completes a task on an unseen API when both channels are empty, and simply putting the fact in the prompt restores success. Availability — not where the fact sits relative to the edit — decides the outcome. A missing fact produces wrong work rather than absent work: the agent fabricates a file or guesses a value instead of reporting itself blocked, and how often it admits it's stuck is a property of the model. Tellingly, a stale convention file costs more than no file, because agents follow the standard even when it prescribes worse code.
stories.why: it's a concrete diagnosis of why coding agents silently go wrong at scale — and a directive for harness builders: guarantee the facts an edit depends on are present when the agent writes, and check that against what it produces, not what it reads.

stories.headline: An agent that invents new crystals in a language of motifs
stories.summary: Data-driven materials discovery is good at interpolating between known structures but rarely invents genuinely new structure types. MatEvolve is an agentic-AI framework — built on Claude Fable 5 with no fine-tuning — that writes each candidate crystal as an interpretable motif profile, a description of the recurring geometric patterns ("motifs") that compose it. Crucially the profile is not just a label but the medium of design: the agent edits the profile, builds a crystal from the edited version, states its rationale, and the most promising candidates are checked with first-principles physics calculations. Applied to rare-earth-lean permanent magnets (strong magnets that avoid scarce, geopolitically fraught rare-earth elements), it reached new structural prototypes more than three times as often as generative models at an equal validation budget, at a comparable rate of on-target magnets.
stories.why: it's a credible case of an agent reaching real novelty in a hard physical-science domain while staying human-readable — the motif profiles expose why a structure works, and the target (rare-earth-lean magnets) speaks directly to materials-supply-chain risk.

stories.headline: Anthropic's annualized revenue reportedly tops $65 billion
stories.summary: Anthropic's annualized revenue reportedly tops $65 billion. Anthropic hit an annualized run-rate above $65B through the end of July — a roughly sevenfold jump year-on-year, said to have added about $18B in run-rate over two months — according to a regular investor update reported by Bloomberg and corroborated by TechCrunch. It is a distinct, concrete revenue figure separate from the earlier reporting on a potential ~$2T IPO valuation; the underlying number rests on unnamed sources.

stories.headline: OpenAI signs a record Ohio data-centre lease, backed by Nvidia
stories.summary: OpenAI signs a record 20-year Ohio data-centre lease, backed by Nvidia. OpenAI leased the "PORTS-Pike" campus in Ohio (about 8GW of IT capacity) for 20 years from an SB Energy (SoftBank) subsidiary; Nvidia is guaranteeing up to $105B of the site's residual value and becomes exclusive chip supplier, and is separately investing about $1.5B in the developer. The Wall Street Journal frames it against roughly $3T of off-balance-sheet AI infrastructure commitments now spread across major tech firms — a scale of leverage worth watching regardless of the headline capacity.

stories.headline: Groq raises $350M at half its former valuation
stories.summary: Groq raises $350M — at half its former valuation. The inference-chip-turned-neocloud startup Groq raised $350M led by Disruptive, with planned Nvidia participation, at a $3.5B valuation — roughly half the $6.9B it carried last September, after Nvidia hired founder-CEO Jonathan Ross and senior staff in a reported $20B licensing deal. Groq disputes the "down round" label, calling $3.5B its post-licensing-deal valuation; either way the price cut is the concrete fact, against ambitions to scale from 54MW toward 200MW-plus of capacity by 2027.

stories.headline: Ukraine launches largest drone barrage on Moscow
stories.summary: Ukraine launched more than 620 drones at the Moscow region overnight into Tuesday 18 August — described by Russia's state agency TASS as the largest drone attack on the capital in two years — while Russian strikes killed at least 10 people in Ukraine's Kharkiv region. Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said air defences destroyed 180 of the drones heading for the capital between Monday evening and 05:00 local time, with 17 more downed later; three people, including a 10-year-old girl, were reported wounded in the Moscow area. On the Ukrainian side, Russian attacks on Kharkiv killed 10 and injured eight, regional officials said.
stories.why: the tempo of long-range drone exchanges is escalating even as diplomatic channels stay frozen, and strikes reaching deep into the Moscow region raise the political stakes for the Kremlin at home.

stories.headline: South Korea seeks command of its own forces
stories.summary: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday 18 August pressed for his country to regain wartime operational control of its own forces, a day after Trump ordered US–South Korea joint military exercises scaled back and said North Korea's Kim Jong Un had responded to his diplomatic outreach. Wartime operational control (OPCON) — authority over Korean troops in a conflict, which has sat with a US-led command since the Korean War — has long been a sovereignty question in Seoul, and Lee framed rebuilding independent capability as the response to a less certain American commitment. Trump ordered the Pentagon to trim the drills on the grounds that Pyongyang had been, in his characterisation, "unthreatening"; South Korean lawmakers called the move "inane" and warned it weakens deterrence, and Trump's claim of a Kim response would mark the first US–North Korea engagement since his first term.
stories.why: a US president loosening a decades-old alliance while courting Pyongyang reshuffles East Asian security calculations for Japan, China and Seoul alike.

stories.headline: Third Crans-Montana fire official charged
stories.summary: A former Crans-Montana security chief became the third official charged over the deadly Constellation fire, Le Temps reported on Tuesday 18 August, with authorities now investigating 16 people in all. The newly charged man, Thibault Beytrison, ran the Valais resort municipality's security between 2017 and 2020 and is to be questioned in late September about gaps in the inspection of public-venue safety; the case concerns the fire at the Constellation establishment that killed people last winter. Cantonal prosecutors are examining whether lax controls contributed to the disaster.
stories.why: the widening roster of charged officials pushes the inquiry from the night of the fire toward the years of oversight decisions that preceded it.

stories.headline: Zambia's Hichilema wins second term
stories.summary: Zambia's incumbent president Hakainde Hichilema won a second term, election authorities confirmed on Tuesday 18 August, after a vote that turned on his economic record. The 64-year-old campaigned on a recovery narrative anchored by a major sovereign-debt restructuring (Zambia was the first African country to default in the pandemic era, and the deal reworked billions in obligations). He now faces pressure to convert that into jobs and lower poverty, while critics accuse his government of growing intolerant of dissent.

stories.headline: Syrian court sentences Assad cousin to death
stories.summary: A Damascus court on Tuesday 18 August sentenced Wassim al-Assad — a cousin of ousted Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad — to death, convicting him of multiple murders and of murder "accompanied by torture and brutality.". Unlike the death sentences handed to Bashar al-Assad and other relatives in absentia on 11 August, Wassim al-Assad is in Syrian custody, making this an enforceable verdict rather than a symbolic one.
stories.why: the new authorities' war-crimes prosecutions are a test of whether post-Assad Syria delivers accountability through courts rather than reprisals.

stories.headline: Migros' Medbase buys Ardentis dental network
stories.summary: Migros-owned health provider Medbase announced on Tuesday 18 August that it is taking a majority stake in the Ardentis dental-clinic chain, expanding its footprint in French-speaking Switzerland. Medbase co-founder and director Marcel Napierala said the move strengthens its presence in Suisse romande and insisted "we are not seeking to maximise our profits." The deal continues the consolidation of Swiss primary and dental care under large retail-linked groups.
stories.why: ownership of everyday clinics by a retail giant shapes where and how patients in Vaud and the wider region access routine care.

stories.headline: Swiss Q2 unemployment ticks up year on year
stories.summary: Switzerland's unemployment rate edged up year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, the Federal Statistical Office reported on Tuesday 18 August, even as the labour market showed signs of stabilising quarter-on-quarter. The jobless rate on the International Labour Organization definition (a survey-based measure counting anyone actively seeking work, broader than the registered-unemployed count) rose to 4.9% from 4.6% a year earlier, with 252,000 people unemployed — 15,000 more than in Q2 2025 — against 5.4 million in work, up 0.8%. But the rate fell back from 5.2% in the first quarter, which the data suggest points to a slight easing.

stories.headline: Trump orders South Korea drills scaled back
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon on Sunday 16 August to sharply scale back the "Ulchi Freedom Shield" military exercises with South Korea, but the drills began on Monday 17 August as planned anyway. Trump called the annual command-post exercises — a decades-old joint drill that Seoul and Washington run each summer — "costly" and said they sent a "totally inappropriate" signal to North Korea, adding that South Korea had failed to help with "the war against Iran" and citing his "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. Those are Trump's characterizations: the exercises are routine and largely computer-simulated, and South Korea's military said the drills "started as planned," a public divergence from the US president's order. Critics quoted by France 24 warned that unilaterally downgrading exercises with a treaty ally could weaken South Korea's defences and reward Pyongyang without any reciprocal concession.
stories.why: it is a concrete step by Washington to soften pressure on North Korea over its allies' objections — the kind of alliance realignment that ripples through European security debates too, including Switzerland's own neutrality argument.

stories.headline: Swiss trio strike gold at the Euros
stories.summary: The first European Athletics Championships ever staged in Great Britain produced Switzerland's finest return at the event: three gold medals and seven in total (three gold, three silver, one bronze), sixth on the final medal table. The golds spanned three very different disciplines — Jason Joseph took the men's 110m hurdles on Wednesday 12 August in a season's-best 13.12 seconds; Angelica Moser retained her women's pole vault title on Thursday 13 August with a season's-best 4.80m; and Audrey Werro won the women's 800m on Friday 14 August in a championship-record 1:54.81, holding off Britain's Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson down the home straight. Simon Ehammer (long jump) and Dominic Lokinyomo Lobalu (10,000m) added silvers.
stories.why: Switzerland is not a country that routinely wins European golds in a hurdles, a jump and a two-lap race in the same week. Beating a reigning Olympic 800m champion for one of them — with a championship record, no less — is the standout: it points to genuine depth in Swiss track and field heading into the rest of the outdoor season.

stories.headline: EU plans tougher Russia sanctions this autumn
stories.summary: EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday 17 August that the bloc will propose "far-reaching" new sanctions against Russia this autumn, aiming to expand the list of sanctioned Russian entities by about a third. Kallas made the announcement after the EU's most recent sanctions package was, by her account, watered down amid member states' pressure to protect national economic interests; she accused Moscow of waging "systematic terror" through its intensifying strikes on Ukrainian cities. The proposal is a plan for the autumn, not yet law — any package needs the unanimous agreement of all 27 member states, the same hurdle that diluted the previous round.
stories.why: sanctions are the EU's main non-military lever on Russia, and the admission that the last package was softened shows how hard unity has become nearly 4½ years into the war — a debate Switzerland tracks closely as it decides how far to mirror EU measures.

stories.headline: Arsenal rout City in Community Shield
stories.summary: Reigning Premier League champions Arsenal beat Manchester City 3-0 in the Community Shield — England's traditional pre-season curtain-raiser, a one-off match that opens the calendar — with goals from Riccardo Calafiori, Kai Havertz and captain Martin Ødegaard. The result is a trophy of modest weight, but the context is not: this was City's first competitive game since Pep Guardiola's exit after a 10-year reign, with new manager Enzo Maresca in charge. Maresca played the outcome down ("It's one game"), but a 3-0 loss to the champions is an uncomfortable start to a rebuild. Arsenal, who won the league last season, looked exactly like a side that means to defend it.
stories.why: The most successful English club of the past decade begins life without the manager who defined it — and the opening evidence is that Arsenal, not City, set the standard the rest of the Premier League must chase this season.

stories.headline: Rodri agrees Barcelona move from City
stories.summary: Barcelona have agreed a deal worth about £65m to sign Spain captain Rodri from Manchester City, according to the BBC. The stage is a club-to-club fee agreed and a four-year contract expected to be signed "in the coming days" — not yet an official completed transfer, so it stays tagged unconfirmed until both clubs announce it. Rodri, 30, won the Ballon d'Or (football's individual player-of-the-year award) in 2024 and was named player of the tournament as Spain won the World Cup this summer; he leaves City, if the deal closes, having won 12 major honours in seven seasons, including the 2022-23 Champions League. City rejected an opening £38.5m Barcelona bid last week, and Real Madrid had earlier looked the likelier destination.
stories.why: Losing their midfield anchor would deepen the rebuild City already face after Guardiola — and hand Barcelona a World Cup-winning holding midfielder at the base of their team.

stories.headline: Thun reach Europa League play-off
stories.summary: FC Thun — who won their first-ever Swiss championship in 2025-26 — lost the away leg 2-3 at Víkingur Reykjavík in Iceland but advanced 5-3 on aggregate after a 3-0 home win in the first leg. That result carries them into the Europa League play-off round and, crucially, guarantees them a place in a European "league phase" for 2026-27 (the 36-team single-table stage UEFA introduced in 2024-25 to replace the old group format). If Thun win the play-off they play in the Europa League; if they lose, they drop into the smaller Conference League — but either way, they are in Europe past Christmas. Their play-off opponent will be Klaksvík (Faroe Islands) or Lech Poznań (Poland). Fellow Swiss sides St. Gallen and Lugano are also alive in the Conference League play-off round.
stories.why: For an unfashionable club that had never been champions until this year, a guaranteed European league-phase campaign is both a sporting milestone and a significant financial windfall — the kind of run that can reshape a small club's budget for years.

stories.headline: Swiatek wins Canadian Open
stories.summary: Iga Swiatek won her first title of the 2026 season, beating world number two Elena Rybakina 6-2 6-3 in the Canadian Open final. It was a commanding performance from the six-time Grand Slam champion — two breaks of serve, two break points saved, a first Canadian Open crown and the 26th title of her career — and it lifts her back into the top five of the rankings. It ends a bruising run for the 25-year-old Pole, who had reached only the fourth round in Paris and the third at Wimbledon this year. "It means so, so much to me because the past months were not easy," she said.
stories.why: With the US Open starting later this month, the form guide just shifted: Swiatek, hunting her first major since Wimbledon last year, has rediscovered her best on hard courts at exactly the right moment.

stories.headline: Djokovic reveals health condition
stories.summary: Novak Djokovic, the 24-time Grand Slam champion, lost to Argentina's Thiago Tirante and afterwards disclosed that he has an ongoing (unspecified) health condition, saying he had struggled in the hot, humid Ohio conditions. It came in a depleted men's event — world number one Jannik Sinner skipped Cincinnati and Carlos Alcaraz withdrew injured — so results here carry an asterisk, but a 38-year-old champion citing a health problem three weeks before the US Open is worth noting rather than reading too much into.
stories.why: It is a small cloud over Djokovic's last Grand Slam tune-up; how serious it proves to be will only become clear at the US Open.

stories.headline: Ukraine launches 600 drones at Russia
stories.summary: Ukraine launched one of its largest aerial attacks of the war overnight into Sunday 16 August, sending hundreds of drones deep into Russia and killing at least six people, while Russian missiles and drones again pounded Ukrainian cities. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said around 600 drones were detected heading for the capital, a third of them shot down over the Moscow region; Russia's Defence Ministry claimed it destroyed 822 Ukrainian drones across the country overnight. In Moscow Oblast an 83-year-old man was killed and a warehouse of the online retailer Wildberries in the village of Koledino was set ablaze, regional governor Andrey Vorobyov said, adding that air defences intercepted 187 drones over the oblast in "one of the most massive" attacks on it in memory. Five more people were killed when over 150 drones hit three towns in the southwestern Rostov region, damaging a railway station and sparking a forest fire. On the Ukrainian side, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian missile strike on Kryvyi Rih killed two and wounded 14, another person was killed in Sumy, and fires broke out across Kyiv — including at a city book market — injuring six. The exchange extends an escalating pattern of long-range strikes now nearly 4½ years into Russia's full-scale invasion, with Ukraine increasingly targeting Russian military industry, energy sites and Wildberries depots.
stories.why: with no ceasefire in sight, both sides are widening deep-strike campaigns that bring the war home to Russian civilians while keeping Ukrainian cities under nightly fire. (AP, 16 Aug 2026; Moscow Oblast detail

stories.headline: Colombia asks Trump to pause tariffs
stories.summary: Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said Saturday 15 August he had asked Donald Trump to temporarily suspend US tariffs on Colombian goods to help businesses recover from the deadly 10 August earthquake, as the death toll neared 294. De la Espriella said he spoke with Trump for about ten minutes and that the US president offered condolences over the magnitude-7.4 quake, which struck near San José del Palmar in the Chocó department at 07:34 local time on Monday 10 August (US Geological Survey). Washington raised its tariff on most Colombian products from 10% to 12.5% in late July, exempting a few goods such as coffee and oil; the president said he asked Trump "to consider temporarily suspending the high tariffs… to give some relief to our business owners." Rescuers, meanwhile, pulled a three-year-old girl alive from the rubble roughly 100 hours after the quake.
stories.why: it links disaster relief to a live trade dispute, and the still-climbing toll shows how much of the mountainous, hard-to-reach epicentre remains under-served days on. (Al Jazeera, 15 Aug 2026; quake parameters

stories.headline: AI agent trained to replicate research papers
stories.summary: Replicating a paper is a good proxy for real research skill: it forces you to fill in the details the authors left implicit, which requires the same hypothesis-driven poking as open-ended work. The authors build Replica, a scalable space of replication tasks, and — the hard part — an auto-generated, rubric-based judge that scores replication quality with low noise and good agreement with human raters, giving a usable reward signal. On top of it they post-train Faraday, a 27B-parameter "AI scientist" that drives coding agents as tools, and report it surpassing Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks, with qualitative traces suggesting a more scientifically-principled approach. Read this alongside "Beyond final scores" above: replication is a real and now largely-automatable slice of research, but it is deliberately not the open-ended discovery that the same week's evaluations say agents still can't do.
stories.why: Reliable, cheap paper-replication would change scientific practice on its own — it is how results get trusted — and a 27B open-ish agent beating the biggest closed models at it is a genuine milestone, hype-adjacent claims notwithstanding.

stories.headline: Heat summer ravages Swiss beech forests
stories.summary: The 2026 heat-and-drought summer is inflicting damage on Swiss forests that long-term monitors say they have never recorded, even as rivers and springs run dry. New field surveys by the Institut für angewandte Pflanzenbiologie (IAP — an applied-plant-biology institute that has monitored Swiss forest health for various cantons since 1974) found that in the beech stands it tracks, two-thirds of the trees are now severely damaged — browning, shedding leaves, or with badly thinned crowns — nearly three times the count after the previous record-heat summer of 2018. The institute's Sabine Braun, who inspects roughly 12,000 trees across 23 cantons each year, said leaves are now drying on the branch and even green ones are "getting sunburnt" — a phenomenon she says she has not seen in 42 years of measurements. Because only about a quarter of the beeches badly hit in 2018 survived, and it is the accumulation of dry years that kills, researchers warn the beech — Switzerland's commonest broadleaf — could all but vanish from the northwest. The drought is visible elsewhere too: Basel's Rhine passenger ferry "Wild Maa" has been beached because the river is too weak to run it, and in peripheral regions springs have dried up, forcing water to be trucked in by tank.
stories.why: forest composition, drinking-water supply and even summer traditions are shifting inside a single season, and the survey turns an abstract "hot summer" into a measured, hard-to-reverse ecological change on the ground. (SRF, 15 Aug 2026; low-Rhine impacts

stories.headline: Ständerat panel strips Bilaterals III wage guard
stories.summary: Switzerland: a Council of States committee reopened the EU-treaty fight by stripping a wage-protection measure from Bilaterals III. On 11 August 2026 the economic-affairs committee of the Ständerat (WAK-S, the upper chamber's economic committee) voted 8–4 with one abstention to drop the fourteenth accompanying wage-protection measure — enhanced dismissal protection for elected employee representatives — arguing it was "not directly connected" to the EU package. The wage-protection measures were the social partners' negotiated price for accepting the package, and unions called the move "a frontal attack" on the deal; the full chamber takes it up in the autumn session. It matters because these are the domestic guarantees that make Bilaterals III — which governs how EU–CH free movement affects work and residence in Switzerland — politically survivable.

stories.headline: Research agents optimize, they don't discover
stories.summary: Leaderboards report an agent's final score on a research task but hide how it got there — where progress was won or lost, and whether the agent learned anything reusable along the way. This work instruments seven frontier models across 36 long-horizon AI R&D tasks with rule-based metrics that dissect each run into Solution Framing, Execution and Feedback Control, and adds controlled tests of whether experience carries over within and across tasks. The findings are pointed: current agents "operate more like engineering optimizers than fully autonomous researchers." They can frame and implement workable solutions, but performance swings widely run-to-run, their strongest solutions mainly adapt or recombine established techniques, and genuine methodological novelty remains rare. The diagnosis is granular — similar final scores can hide very different bottlenecks, and accumulated "experience" sometimes misleads later decisions.
stories.why: It is the measured counterweight to "AI scientist" hype (see Cross-cutting thread 1): it says exactly what today's agents can and can't do, and turns the gap into concrete engineering targets rather than a vibe.

stories.headline: Symmetry explains sudden learning and scaling
stories.summary: Networks trained by smooth gradient descent often learn in steps — the loss sits on a plateau, then drops abruptly — yet training curves aggregate into smooth power laws; both behaviours show up in architectures with wildly different internals, hinting at a few hidden "collective variables" doing the real work. This paper shows a symmetry pins down what those variables are. Because a layer is a sum over interchangeable units, relabelling the units leaves it unchanged; that symmetry, plus smoothness, forces a universal leading form near the small initial weights — a quadratic term in which every architectural detail is compressed into a single "structure matrix" $A(x)$ the authors compute per architecture. Perceptrons, attention, mixtures-of-experts and convolutions then become one model at different $A$, whose dynamics reduce (when the data share an eigenbasis) to a Lotka–Volterra equation — the classic predator–prey system — in which learning "modes" switch on one after another. Smaller initial weights spread the switch-on times into visible plateaus; when many modes blur together, the same events merge into a power law whose exponent the theory predicts, confirmed numerically across methods and architectures.
stories.why: It offers a genuine unifying explanation for two of deep learning's most-discussed mysteries — emergent "grokking"-style jumps and smooth scaling laws — as two faces of one symmetry-fixed dynamics.

stories.headline: Swiss motion pushes local tech procurement
stories.summary: A Vaud Green MP will ask federal commissioners next week to steer Switzerland's public IT spending toward Swiss and European suppliers rather than US ones. National Councillor Sophie Michaud Gigon (Greens, Vaud) told Le Temps she will defend a motion in the powerful Commission for Economic Affairs and Taxation on 17 or 18 August, arguing that Bern spends hundreds of millions of francs a year on digital services — often American — that Swiss firms could provide, and that this contradicts the "digital sovereignty" strategy the Confederation itself adopted in 2025. Swiss providers Proton and Infomaniak back the text. Motions of this kind have failed before, and the proposal now has to survive the commission and both chambers, so it is a starting pressure point rather than a settled rule.
stories.why: it puts a concrete, procurement-level lever behind the much-repeated "digital sovereignty" slogan — the kind of measure that would actually redirect money and reduce dependence on US cloud vendors, of direct interest to anyone working in Swiss software.

stories.headline: Trump vows to declare Hormuz US territory
stories.summary: The Iran war's newest flashpoint is a claim with no basis in the law of the sea: Trump says he will declare the Strait of Hormuz US "territory.". US President Donald Trump said on 14 August 2026 he intends to declare the strait — the ~40-km-wide waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through — American "territory," repeating "pretty soon" in a 15 August update. No state can annex an international strait: the Strait of Hormuz lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters and is governed by the transit-passage regime of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, so treat "US territory" as a political assertion from an administration whose Hormuz claims have repeatedly outrun the facts, not a legal reality. Separately, French- and English-language outlets reported acute strain on the carrier USS Abraham Lincoln after nine months at sea.

stories.headline: Magnitude-7.7 quake hits eastern Indonesia
stories.summary: A magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck eastern Indonesia on 15 August 2026, killing at least 20. The quake hit in the morning (local time), with early reports of collapsed buildings and people fleeing into the streets; the toll was still preliminary as rescue efforts began.

stories.headline: A record-dry summer bites Switzerland
stories.summary: A record-hot, rain-starved summer is now biting Switzerland directly. Through mid-August, Swiss and regional reporting described the Rhine dropping to levels that idled a Basel ferry and forced dredging debates, cantons coordinating how to share water with neighbours, and continued alpine glacier loss ("it's shocking how much has melted"), against the backdrop of a large forest fire in Germany that evacuated ~1,800 people on 13 August.

stories.headline: Dense credit for multi-turn RL agents
stories.summary: Training tool-using agents with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR — the reward is a checkable success/failure, not a learned score) has a stubborn flaw: a whole multi-turn trajectory earns a single reward, so the method can't tell which turns actually mattered — the credit-assignment problem. Pure imitation of a stronger "teacher" model gives dense per-token guidance but caps the student at the teacher's ability and can collapse training. CrEST splits the difference with a two-level scheme: it computes turn-segmented verified advantages to fix credit between turns, then uses an entropy-gated "self-teacher" (the model supervising itself, engaged only where it is uncertain) to refine credit within a turn. Crucially, the teacher's job is demoted from choosing the direction of each weight update to merely scaling its magnitude — which keeps RLVR's verifier-bounded performance ceiling while adding dense signal. On the BFCL V3 and WildToolBench tool-use benchmarks it beats both RL and distillation baselines at two model sizes, with the biggest gains on the longest trajectories.
stories.why: It is a concrete recipe for giving agents useful feedback on which of their many steps earned a success, without capping them at a teacher's skill — the bottleneck for training on long, real tasks.

stories.headline: Swiss GDP rebounds on pharma exports
stories.summary: Swiss GDP rebounded sharply in the second quarter of 2026, growing 1.5% in a first estimate from the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), after 0.4% in Q1. SECO attributed the jump to a strong recovery in the chemical and pharmaceutical industry — the country's largest export sector — whose exports rose 15.2% quarter-on-quarter after four straight quarters of decline; broader industrial exports grew 1.7%. SECO issued only a brief flash release and will publish detailed figures on 3 September.
stories.why: the headline looks strong, but much of it is one narrow, volatile sector: a large part of the pharma bounce reflects shipments front-loaded ahead of US tariffs (Washington set an import levy of 12.5% on Swiss goods at the end of July), so the reader should treat 1.5% as a preliminary, lopsided figure rather than proof of broad-based strength — the industry lobby Swissmem has warned that recent industrial growth rests "on a small number of companies."

stories.headline: Eval-awareness probe measures the prompt, not the model
stories.summary: A model that acts differently when it senses an evaluation would quietly corrupt the evals we trust, so researchers have tried to read that "sense" straight from activations: contrast the model's internal state on prompts that announce a test against prompts that don't, extract the difference as a direction, and report how cleanly it separates held-out cases — then compare that score across models and correlate it with scale. The catch, the author shows, is that "a prompt that announces an evaluation" is not one prompt but a choice among many, and the method never pins down which.
stories.why: holding the task fixed and varying only that unstated choice, both the headline score and even the direction in which it trends with model size follow the prompt rather than the model. It's a clean warning that a widely cited interpretability result may be an artifact of prompt selection — exactly the kind of honest self-check the safety-eval literature needs.

stories.headline: SAE ablation scores depend on where you measure
stories.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) try to name the concepts a model computes; the usual test of whether a discovered feature matters is to switch it off and see what changes. But a feature fires at many tokens, and the effect must be read at one of them — and the convention (measure where the feature fires hardest) means the dictionary being evaluated picks the measurement point. Take two SAEs Google released for the same model, match their features by similarity, and even near-identical features get measured at different tokens.
stories.why: two dictionaries "compared" under the standard protocol are often not being measured on the same footing at all, so leaderboard-style SAE comparisons can reward measurement choices rather than better features. It's a distinct paper from the earlier "which SAE you trained decides causality" line, but it points the same way: interpretability's evaluation plumbing needs auditing before its scores can be trusted.

stories.headline: White House accuses 40 nations over China tariffs
stories.summary: The White House accused more than 40 countries of helping China dodge US tariffs, in a report its trade office published on Thursday 13 August. The Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy — headed by trade adviser Peter Navarro — said Chinese goods are routed through third countries and relabelled to disguise their origin, a practice it branded the "Great Transshipment Scam" and estimated costs the US Treasury 19–26 billion dollars a year in lost tariff revenue. It named the EU, Mexico, Canada, India, Japan and South Korea as the biggest "enablers," alongside Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia and Cambodia.
stories.why: the "scam" framing and the dollar figures are the administration's own, and the legal footing is contested — the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in February, and 25 Democratic-led states are challenging the replacement levies in court as a pretext to reimpose them; none of the named governments had responded, so read the report as a negotiating move to pressure trading partners, not a settled finding.

stories.headline: Colombia quake toll tops 200
stories.summary: The death toll from the magnitude-7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia on Monday 10 August has climbed past 200, with more than 2,500 injured, as rescue teams moved into what officials call a final search phase. The UN said on Wednesday 12 August that it was still scaling up assistance two days after the quake, whose epicentre lay in the Chocó–Buenaventura area along the Pacific coast; humanitarian assessments continue in the hardest-hit zones around Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdó, where damage to communications, transport and public services is hampering relief. UNICEF, active in Chocó for over two decades, said it had reached 22,000 people with hygiene and water-storage kits and warned that children face "growing risks" as schools and homes lie damaged and essential services stay disrupted. Two days earlier the confirmed toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, so the figures roughly doubled as crews reached collapsed buildings and cut-off communities.
stories.why: this is Colombia's deadliest earthquake in decades, and the concentration of damage in the poorer Pacific-coast departments — where the state has a thin footprint — means recovery will test the national response long after the rescue window closes.

stories.headline: Putin visits disputed Kuril Islands
stories.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin made the first-ever visit by a Russian or Soviet leader to the disputed Kuril Islands, drawing a formal protest from Japan on Thursday 13 August. Putin toured a fish-processing plant on Iturup (known as Etorofu in Japan), one of four islands Tokyo claims as its "Northern Territories" and which the Soviet Union seized at the end of World War II in 1945, deporting some 17,000 Japanese residents; about 20,000 Russian citizens live there now. Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi called the visit "absolutely unacceptable" and lodged a protest through diplomatic channels. The unresolved sovereignty dispute is the reason Moscow and Tokyo never signed a formal post-war peace treaty, and relations have deteriorated further since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
stories.why: a sitting president planting himself on the contested islands is a deliberate signal that Moscow considers the question closed, hardening a territorial dispute that has blocked normal Russia–Japan relations for eight decades.

stories.headline: Lebanon abolishes death penalty
stories.summary: Lebanon's parliament abolished the death penalty on Tuesday 11 August, making the country the first Arab state — and the first in the Middle East — to strike capital punishment from its books. A majority of the 128-seat assembly backed the bill after amendments, with the bloc of the Iran-aligned Shia movement Hezbollah the notable exception, according to the speaker's office. The law replaces death sentences with life imprisonment at hard labour; Lebanon had already observed an unofficial moratorium on executions since 2004, and the Justice Ministry's prisons directorate counted 85 people under death sentence at the end of 2025, whose sentences now fall to be commuted. Rights groups have long pressed Arab governments — most of which retain and use capital punishment — to follow the global abolition trend.
stories.why: in a region where the death penalty is near-universal and often used for political and drug offences, a full legislative abolition sets a first regional precedent that campaigners will cite elsewhere, even as the change is legal rather than a shift in the underlying justice system.

stories.headline: Wandering black hole feeds on gravitational wake
stories.summary: Supermassive black holes are thought to grow from "intermediate-mass" seeds of a few thousand to a few hundred thousand suns — and theory says many such seeds never make it to a galaxy's centre, instead wandering through their host after galaxy mergers fail to drag them inward. A nagging problem: a black hole parked in a galaxy's centre has gas funnelled onto it, but a wanderer drifting through thin interstellar gas shouldn't have much to eat. This team reports evidence for a wandering black hole of ~35,000 solar masses that is feeding anyway — by capturing gas from the dense wake its own gravity piles up behind it as it plows through the interstellar medium (the same gravitational-focusing effect that lets a moving mass gather a trailing overdensity). Multi-epoch spectroscopy resolves three gas components — a thin inflow ahead of the hole, a dense redshifted wake behind it, and thick absorbers close in that make its light flicker — matching the predicted geometry.
stories.why: it is the first direct observational evidence for a fuel source that had only been predicted on paper, and it means these elusive middleweight black holes can grow while adrift — a channel that helps explain how the giants at galaxy centres got so big.

stories.headline: Car bomb kills Haftar intelligence chief
stories.summary: A car bomb killed Fawzi al-Mansouri, the military intelligence chief of Libya's eastern-based forces, in Benghazi on Tuesday 11 August — a rare high-level assassination inside the stronghold of commander Khalifa Haftar. The device detonated as al-Mansouri's car left evening prayers in the al-Hawari district; Haftar had appointed him to lead military intelligence in May 2024. No group claimed responsibility, and Khaled Haftar, the commander's son, said an investigation had opened and that "indicators point to a despicable terrorist tactic." The killing came the same day drones struck oil facilities in the divided country's east. Libya has been split since 2014 between the Haftar-led east and a UN-recognised government in Tripoli.
stories.why: a strike this deep inside Haftar's security apparatus signals cracks in the east's tight internal control and complicates the stalled effort to reunify Libya's rival administrations.

stories.headline: Quadrupolar order drives hydride superconductor
stories.summary: Lanthanum hydride (LaH₁₀) is the poster child of hydride superconductors — materials that carry current with zero resistance at a record-high 250 K (about −23 °C), but only when squeezed to ~170 GPa, roughly 1.7 million times atmospheric pressure. Everyone knew that as you compress it, its crystal changes shape (an R‑3m → Fm‑3m structural transition) right where superconductivity switches on, but why was unclear. This French–Japanese team ran the numbers — using a machine-learned interatomic potential (a neural network trained on quantum-mechanical energies, standing in for far slower first-principles simulation) — and found the transition is governed by a quadrupolar order parameter: the hydrogen atoms collectively adopt a subtle, four-lobed distortion pattern (think of the symmetry of a cloverleaf rather than a simple stretch). That "hidden order" softens a specific set of lattice vibrations (T₂g phonons) that happen to couple strongly to electrons — and strong electron–phonon coupling is exactly what glues electrons into the pairs that superconduct.
stories.why: it hands materials designers a concrete knob — look for compounds with these soft quadrupolar distortions — in the hunt for a superconductor that works at everyday pressures, the field's holy grail.

stories.headline: Bats socially learn winter hibernation sites
stories.summary: Every autumn, temperate-zone bats fly long distances to gather at specific caves and mines to hibernate (the sites are called hibernacula). Biologists have long suspected each generation learns these locations from older bats rather than finding them by instinct — but hard evidence was missing. Researchers compiled 30,882 observations spanning 1985–2023 of 13,852 banded greater mouse-eared bats (Myotis myotis) and found four independent lines of evidence for social transmission: which hibernaculum an individual ends up using tracks the bats it associated with at summer roosts, not simply the nearest site or its birthplace. It is one of the longest-baseline datasets ever brought to bear on the question of animal "culture."
stories.why: if bats inherit migration knowledge socially rather than genetically, losing the older, knowledgeable individuals in a colony — to disease like white-nose syndrome or to disturbance of a single cave — can erase a route the population can't quickly relearn, a real consideration for European conservation.

stories.headline: How some escape a genetic Alzheimer's fate
stories.summary: In an extended Colombian family, thousands of people carry a single mutation (PSEN1 E280A) that all but guarantees early-onset Alzheimer's in their 40s — making them a natural experiment for the disease. A few members are mysteriously spared for decades, and the standout case, a man carrying a rare variant nicknamed RELN‑COLBOS, stayed dementia-free ~20 years past the expected onset. This team dissected the entorhinal cortex — the memory-circuit region where Alzheimer's pathology typically begins — in protected and unprotected carriers using single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics (techniques that read which genes are switched on, cell by cell and in place within the tissue) plus whole-genome sequencing. They report that resilience looks oligogenic — the combined effect of several rare variants rather than one — and find unusual cell populations in the protected brain: RELN‑positive inhibitory interneurons enriched in the cortex's top layer and abundant ADAMTSL1‑positive excitatory neurons, hinting at a preserved, rewired local circuit.
stories.why: people who resist a disease they are genetically fated to get are the best possible pointer to a treatment; mapping the cells and genes behind their protection is how you turn a lucky biology into a drug target. As a single-family preprint, it is a mechanistic lead, not proof.

stories.headline: DESI Legacy Survey maps four billion objects
stories.summary: The DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team released the newest and largest version of its map of the sky — 13 years in the making, covering three-quarters of the entire sky and cataloguing nearly four billion distinct objects: stars, galaxies, supernovae, gravitational lenses and more. The imaging comes from two U.S. National Science Foundation telescopes at Kitt Peak (Mayall) and Cerro Tololo in Chile (Blanco), the latter carrying the U.S. Department of Energy's Dark Energy Camera (DECam). The full catalogue is public, and it is the same imaging that selects targets for the DESI spectroscopic survey mapping cosmic expansion.
stories.why: a free, sky-spanning catalogue of this depth is raw material for years of discovery — it is the finding chart the whole community, and increasingly automated surveys, mines for everything from rare lensed quasars to the next transient.

stories.headline: JWST reads a young super-Jupiter's chemistry
stories.summary: AF Lep b is one of the nearest young giant planets we can study directly — 3–4 Jupiter masses, orbiting ~9 AU (about Saturn's distance) from its star. Using JWST spectroscopy from 2.85–5.3 microns, the team detected carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, methane, carbon monoxide (including its heavier ¹³CO isotope) and water in its atmosphere. Letting carbon, oxygen and sulfur abundances vary independently in the atmospheric fit — sulfur is a newer, powerful tracer because it is locked into dust and rock — they find the planet enriched ~3–5× above its star. That sulfur signature implies the planet swallowed roughly 56 Earth masses of solid material (ice and rock) as it formed, and its carbon-to-oxygen ratio points to formation near where it now sits rather than in the frigid outer disk.
stories.why: sulfur is emerging as a "formation fingerprint," and here it lets astronomers reconstruct how a giant planet was built — a directly-imaged analog to the metal-enrichment story of Jupiter itself.

stories.headline: Faster estimate of quantum state entropy
stories.summary: The von Neumann entropy of a quantum state is its information-theoretic "temperature gauge" — it measures how mixed or uncertain the state is (zero for a pristine, fully-known state; large for a noisy or highly entangled one), and estimating it underlies benchmarking quantum computers and certifying entanglement. The catch: you can't read a quantum state off like a number; you have to prepare many identical copies and measure them, and every known method needed a number of copies growing as the square of the state's dimension d (written Ω(d²)) — a wall that plug-in estimators provably cannot beat. This paper gives the first estimator that breaks that quadratic barrier, needing o(d²) copies (asymptotically fewer than d²) for fixed accuracy, via a new "pinching" inequality plus tailored estimators for large and small eigenvalues.
stories.why: copies of a quantum state are expensive to make, so shaving the sample cost of a routine diagnostic makes verifying real quantum hardware measurably cheaper — the first improvement on a bound that had stood as a hard limit.
stories.affiliation_label: Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University

stories.headline: Meta returns with open Muse Glimmer
stories.summary: Meta returns to open weights with Muse Glimmer, a 30B multimodal agent model. After more than a year without an open release, Meta published Muse-Glimmer-30B (29.8B parameters, Apache-2.0) — the first open model from its new Superintelligence Labs — a multimodal (image-and-text-in) model built for agentic tool use that fits in under ~20 GB of memory once its weights are compressed, i.e. runnable on consumer hardware. A companion essay from Mark Zuckerberg defends distilling other labs' models and argues for fewer restrictions on US labs — read widely as a shot at OpenAI and Anthropic — and an open-weight Muse Spark 1.2 is reported to follow. Meta / Hugging Face model card
stories.why: an Apache-2.0 multimodal agent model that runs locally is directly useful to developers, and Meta re-entering the open field resets the competitive floor. The distillation defense is notable given how much of this cycle's research (above) is about distilling expensive models into cheap ones.

stories.headline: M7.4 quake devastates western Colombia
stories.summary: A magnitude-7.4 earthquake devastated western Colombia on Monday 10 August, killing scores of people and triggering a frantic overnight search for survivors under collapsed buildings. The US Geological Survey put the quake at M7.4, striking 5 km south of San José del Palmar in the remote Chocó region at 12:34 UTC, followed by a M5.0 aftershock and, per Colombia's Geological Service, at least 21 aftershocks by late Monday. President Abelardo de la Espriella — sworn in only on Friday 7 August — reported 35 dead in Cali and declared a state of emergency; local authorities counted at least 40 more dead around Pereira and a dozen elsewhere, with 700 injured in the Valle del Cauca department alone. Roughly 1,600 buildings were damaged, including hospital floors in Cali that collapsed onto patients and the towers of a historic cathedral in Manizales. More than 2,700 people were "reported missing" on citizen-run websites by Monday night, a figure authorities caution is unverified and not a confirmed count. Chocó, near the epicentre and reachable mainly by boat or plane, remains largely unassessed.
stories.why: it is Colombia's strongest quake in decades, striking a mountainous, hard-to-reach zone where the true toll may take days to emerge, and the first major test of a government four days into office.

stories.headline: Distilled skill beats reasoning mode
stories.summary: Reasoning models — the ones that "think out loud" before answering — beat their plain counterparts on multi-step agent tasks but pay a 3–6× premium in output tokens, much of it spent re-deriving the same procedures episode after episode. The authors have a coding agent read a small set of past trajectories from a training split and compile them into a compact natural-language "skill" — a paragraph of instructions injected into a non-reasoning model's system prompt. On-policy distillation (learning from the model's own attempts rather than a fixed dataset) is the broader family this belongs to.
stories.why: across four agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, τ²-bench telecom and retail, SpreadsheetBench-Verified), the skill recovers 55%–100%+ of the reasoning gap for GPT-5.4-mini on held-out tasks — beating reasoning mode outright on two of four — while emitting 2.7–6× fewer output tokens and zero reasoning tokens. It suggests much of what "thinking" buys is reusable and can be cached as text, not re-paid every call.

stories.headline: Assad sentenced to death in absentia
stories.summary: A Damascus criminal court on Tuesday 11 August sentenced Syria's ex-president Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for premeditated murder, torture and crimes against humanity committed during the country's nearly 14-year war. His brother Maher al-Assad — like Bashar, now in exile in Russia — was also sentenced to death in absentia, while cousin Atef Najib, the former head of political security in Deraa who was detained in January 2025, heard his death sentence from inside a courtroom cage. Najib launched the 2011 crackdown on Deraa protesters that helped ignite the uprising and later civil war; the court cited "the intentional killing of children under 15" among his crimes. Presiding judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan said testimony established Assad as "the highest decision-maker" who used state institutions to facilitate the crimes.
stories.why: it is the first ruling by Syria's post-Assad transitional authorities against the former ruling family, and — though the two principals are beyond reach in Russia — sets a legal precedent for prosecuting the old government's officials.

stories.headline: Netanyahu rejects US-backed Gaza roadmap
stories.summary: On Sunday 9 August 2026 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told a cabinet meeting that "Israel rejects the 15-point document" — the US-backed Gaza roadmap that Hamas agreed to in late July — insisting the military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.". Netanyahu spelled out that this meant "heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry," and said Israel remains in talks with Washington despite its objections, calling President Donald Trump "our greatest friend in the White House" while adding, "We know how to stand our ground on these matters." The plan, drawn up by Trump's "Board of Peace," calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas surrenders its weapons, after which an International Stabilization Force and a new Palestinian police force would secure Gaza; Hamas has pointedly avoided the word "disarmament," saying it agreed to place weapons in storage under a US-backed Palestinian technocratic administration and that implementation also depends on Israel withdrawing and halting attacks. The rejection is the sharpest public break yet between the two allies, and it lands weeks before Israel's 27 October election — the country's first national vote since the October 2023 Hamas-led attacks — with far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich welcoming the move and declaring the army "cannot withdraw even a millimetre." More than 1,250 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since a US-mediated ceasefire in October 2025, according to Gaza health officials, while Israeli forces still control large parts of the enclave and most of its 2 million-plus residents remain displaced.
stories.why: Netanyahu is publicly refusing the very roadmap Trump touted as a breakthrough, and by naming full disarmament-before-withdrawal as his red line — hardened by election-year pressure from his coalition's right — he leaves the ceasefire framework's core sequencing stalled.

stories.headline: Vollering wins second Tour de France Femmes
stories.summary: The race that opened on Swiss roads a week earlier ended with a show of force. Dutchwoman Demi Vollering (FDJ United–SUEZ) attacked 16 km from the finish of the closing stage in Nice, dropped her main rival and rode in alone to seal the overall title — the biggest prize in women's cycling — for the second time after 2023. Poland's Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney held on to second at 1 minute 18 seconds, with Italy's Elisa Longo Borghini third. The Swiss story was a painful one: Marlen Reusser (Movistar) — one of the world's best riders against the clock, and the winner of this Tour's individual time trial — crashed roughly 60 km from the line on the final stage and, though she remounted, slid to 14th overall, her podium hopes gone in an instant. Compatriot Noemi Rüegg, fourth after the opening weekend, faded out of the top ten as the mountains bit.
stories.why: A dominant winner and a cruel Swiss near-miss in the same afternoon — Reusser had ridden herself into podium contention before a single crash on the last day undid nine stages of work, the kind of fine margin that defines stage racing.

stories.headline: Syria, Russia recast military-base deal
stories.summary: Syria's Foreign Ministry announced on Sunday 9 August 2026 that Damascus and Moscow had signed a memorandum of understanding reorganising Russia's military presence on the Syrian coast, ending about 18 months of negotiations over the future of the Hmeimim air base and the Tartous naval facility. Under the deal, Syria will take over management of the sites designated for civilian use — including Hmeimim Airport and the fourth commercial berth at Tartous Port — for gradual integration into civilian administration, while the facilities still used militarily are to be converted into "joint training and qualification centres." The ministry set a deadline of no more than three months to complete the transition and called the agreement the most significant step since the talks began, opening "a new phase" in Syrian-Russian relations. Tartous and Hmeimim are Russia's only military bases outside the former Soviet Union; Moscow used them to prop up Bashar al-Assad, who was overthrown in December 2024 and now lives in exile in Russia, and President Ahmad al-Sharaa — who led the Islamist-rebel alliance that toppled Assad — has since met President Vladimir Putin twice while Damascus presses for Assad's extradition.
stories.why: the memorandum lets post-Assad Syria assert sovereignty over strategic coastal infrastructure while preserving a reduced Russian foothold — a pragmatic bargain that keeps Moscow's Mediterranean access alive even after it lost its patron in Damascus.

stories.headline: Lugano lead Super League after three rounds
stories.summary: Three rounds into the Swiss season and the pacesetter is not one of the country's traditional heavyweights but FC Lugano, the club from Italian-speaking Ticino. A 2-0 home win over FC Zürich — a Kevin Behrens double inside 18 first-half minutes — left Lugano the only side with a perfect nine points and a 11-2 goal difference, and unbeaten across six competitive matches once European qualifiers are counted. Behind them the picture shuffled: record champions Young Boys, who had scored 10 goals in their first two games, threw away a 2-0 lead to draw 2-2 at Lausanne after Edimilson Fernandes was sent off just before the hour; Basel, beaten on the opening weekends, steadied themselves by beating last season's surprise champions Thun 4-2, with Djibril Sow scoring twice and setting up two more. It remains far too early to call a title race in a league that runs to next May, but the early order has again been inverted — the biggest names chasing a side most had pencilled in, at best, as outside contenders.
stories.why: In a league usually carved up between Young Boys, Basel and a few others, the team sitting top after a month is a modestly-resourced Ticino club playing the most convincing football in the country — a reminder that the Swiss top flight is more open than its budgets suggest.

stories.headline: Car bomb hits Colombia after new president
stories.summary: A car bomb exploded at a highway toll plaza in Colombia's southwestern Cauca department on Saturday 8 August 2026, one day after right-wing political newcomer Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as president. The device detonated at a toll station on the Pan-American Highway — the main road artery of Colombia's southwest — wounding two security guards; no deaths were reported. The army attributed the attack to two dissident factions of the former FARC (Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, the guerrilla army that demobilised under a 2016 peace accord), splinter groups that rejected that deal and remain active in Cauca. De la Espriella, a lawyer who campaigned on a hard-line security platform, took office in Cali on Friday 7 August, succeeding the leftist Gustavo Petro. "Colombia will not kneel before violence, nor will it allow the destruction of the infrastructure that connects our regions," Transport Minister Elsa Noguera said.
stories.why: the bombing is an immediate security test for a president elected on promises of a tougher line against armed groups, and it signals the dissidents' capacity to strike national infrastructure at the very start of his term.

stories.headline: Iran sets conditions to reopen Hormuz
stories.summary: Iran's Supreme National Security Council set six conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, its secretary said in remarks reported Saturday 8 August 2026, a day before President Masoud Pezeshkian said "now is the best time" for a deal with the United States. The strait — the narrow chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil passes — has been shut to commercial shipping amid the Iran–US confrontation that opened earlier in 2026. Council secretary Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr said it would reopen only once Washington ends threats and what he called "insults" to Iran, permanently halts attacks on Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq, lifts what he termed a US naval blockade and pulls its forces back from the region, pays compensation for two "imposed wars", lifts sanctions, and releases frozen Iranian assets. "The Supreme National Security Council will never back down, neither in war nor in negotiations," he said. Pezeshkian, on Sunday 9 August, struck a more conciliatory note, saying Iran should move beyond a state of "neither war nor peace" and needed a dispute-resolution mechanism rather than a return to fighting.
stories.why: the list formalises and broadens Iran's terms — explicitly extending its red lines to Yemen and Iraq — and the daylight between the council's maximalism and the president's opening reflects the internal split that will shape whether the standoff eases or hardens.

stories.headline: Saudi, Turkey, Pakistan sign Mecca defence pact
stories.summary: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a trilateral mutual-defence pact in Mecca on Friday 7 August, pledging that an armed attack on any one of the three will be treated as an attack on all. Signed at Al-Safa Palace by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, the "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement" was announced in identical statements by Pakistan's Foreign Ministry and Turkey's presidential communications office: it is "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression" and to deepen defence cooperation across the three states. A Turkish official, speaking anonymously, called the deal "purely defensive in nature" and "not against" any specific country; Turkish media said it is likely to enable joint exercises, technology transfers and intelligence-sharing. The pact extends the bilateral Saudi–Pakistan defence agreement of September 2025 to include Turkey, and lands during the wider regional war with Iran that opened in February 2026, in which Gulf states have come under repeated missile and drone fire.
stories.why: it binds together the Muslim world's only nuclear-armed state (Pakistan), the holder of NATO's second-largest army (Turkey) and the Gulf's richest economy (Saudi Arabia) into a self-defence bloc — a significant regional realignment whose implicit nuclear dimension India and Israel will both read closely.

stories.headline: AI beats models at cyclone forecasting
stories.summary: WeatherNext Cyclones (WN-C) is a deployed AI weather model that generates large ensemble forecasts (many simulated scenarios, giving calibrated uncertainty) for tropical-cyclone track, intensity and size worldwide out to 15 days, trained on global reanalysis plus a historical cyclone database. Evaluated on 2023–2025 storms, it delivers roughly a day or more of lead-time advantage over leading operational physics models — a jump comparable to about a decade of conventional progress — while running on input data orders of magnitude coarser than regional models, implying that very high resolution is not required for state-of-the-art intensity prediction. Because it is peer-reviewed and operationally evaluated rather than a blog-post benchmark, it is also a clean case study in ensemble evaluation methodology and the "coarse data is enough" lesson.
stories.why: It is production, operationally evaluated ML beating established numerical models on a high-stakes, life-safety forecasting task — and a template for how "AI weather" claims should be validated.

stories.headline: 25 US states sued the Trump administration over its new tariffs
stories.summary: The suit, filed 3 August 2026 in the US Court of International Trade, argues the double-digit tariffs imposed last month under a "forced-labour" rationale are an illegal workaround of the "Liberation Day" tariffs the Supreme Court struck down in February. The White House called the tariffs "appropriate and legal" — a self-characterisation that should be read against that February courtroom loss. Switzerland is among the economies caught in the same tariff push.

stories.headline: Zelensky visits Serbia as strikes hit Kyiv
stories.summary: Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky made the first visit by a Ukrainian president to Serbia — a Moscow-aligned state — meeting President Aleksandar Vucic in Belgrade on Friday 7 August, even as a fresh Russian barrage killed three near Kyiv overnight into Saturday. The two leaders discussed expanding economic ties, Serbia's EU path and security; the trip is read as symbolic, given Belgrade's traditional closeness to Russia and its careful balancing act since 2022. Overnight, Russia fired six Iskander-M ballistic missiles plus S-400 missiles at the Kyiv region, none of which were shot down; the strike on Brovary district killed a grandmother, grandfather and their three-year-old grandson, regional officials said. The visit comes days after UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the deadliest strikes on Kyiv this year — 17 killed on 6 August — as part of an "alarming pattern" and "a clear violation of international humanitarian law."
stories.why: Ukraine is courting even Russia's friends for diplomatic cover as its air defences visibly fail against intensifying strikes.

stories.headline: Houthi attacks kill dozens of Yemeni troops
